summary: Updates RFC 4326 to clarify and update the allocation rules for the ULE Next-Header registry, which is used by ULE and Generic Stream Encapsulation to record extension headers and protocols.

eli5.summary: A list of labels needs clear rules for who may add a new one. This document updates those rules.

questions: what is the ule next-header registry
how are ule next-header values allocated
which ule next-header values are for private use
what is the difference between mandatory and optional ule extension headers
subtitle: Clearer rules for who can add entries to the ULE Next-Header registry, now shared by ULE and GSE.

tldr.problem: The ULE Next-Header registry, created by RFC 4326, was also needed by the DVB Generic Stream Encapsulation (GSE), and its allocation rules and encoding needed clarifying.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7280 makes new entries follow the Specification Required policy with Designated Expert review, splits the 0-511 space into mandatory and optional ranges, reserves 144-159 for private use, and adds an explanatory note to the registry.
tldr.outcome: Anyone proposing a new extension header knows what to supply, and experimenters have a private range. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4326.

today: RFC 7280 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4326, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. Its allocation rules replace those in Section 11 of RFC 4326.

sections.title: Why the Rules Were Updated
sections.content:
The Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE, RFC 4326) carries IP datagrams over links that use the MPEG-2 Transport Stream. Its header has a Type field that identifies payload types and Extension Headers, and RFC 4326 asked IANA to keep a ULE Next-Header registry of the values behind that field.

The Digital Video Broadcast (DVB) Project later published the Generic Stream Encapsulation (GSE) for second-generation DVB physical layers. GSE shares many network properties with ULE and uses a common Type field format (RFC 5163), so the same registry applies to it.

RFC 7280 therefore updates Section 11.1 of RFC 4326 in four ways: it clarifies use by GSE as well as ULE, requires the Specification Required policy, reserves a range for private use, and adds an explanatory note to the registry.
sections.eli5: Two sibling systems use the same label board, so the board needed clearer rules that work for both.

sections.title: How Registry Values Map to Type Values
sections.content:
Mandatory Extension Headers use registry values in the decimal range 0-255. The registered value corresponds to a 16-bit Type value, made by setting the most significant 8 bits to zero. That Type value can identify a Mandatory Extension Header or a specific protocol.

Optional Extension Headers use the range 256-511. The registered value corresponds to the 16-bit Type value that would be used for an Optional Extension Header with a length (H-LEN) of 1.

The RFC gives an informative example with the padding Extension Header. Value 256 (hex 0x100) is used for a 2-byte padding header, where H-LEN is 1. A 6-byte padding header has H-LEN 3, giving Type value 768 (hex 0x300). The H-LEN sits in bits 5 to 7 of the Type field and is combined with bits 8 to 15 of the registered value.
sections.eli5: The board stores one 'base' label for each envelope kind. When you pick the actual envelope size, the system combines the base label with the size to make the final label.

sections.title: The Allocation Policy
sections.content:
New allocations are assigned by IANA under the Specification Required policy of RFC 5226. An application must reference a 'permanent and readily available public specification' of the Next-Header extension. An IETF Standards Track RFC can serve, and other specifications are also permitted. A Designated Expert advises IANA on whether a specification qualifies.

The registry covers 0-511 decimal (0x0000-0x01FF), and IANA must not allocate values above 511. For each value the registry also records the allowed H-LEN values. Together, the value and H-LEN give ULE and GSE a set of allowed 16-bit values in the range 0-1535 decimal.

The registry has two ranges. Values 0-255 indicate Mandatory Extension Headers (or link-dependent Type fields). Values 256-511 indicate Optional Extension Headers, and an entry there MUST define the need for the Optional Extension and its intended use.
sections.eli5: To add a new label you must show a written, public description of it, and a referee checks that the description is good enough.

sections.title: What the Expert Checks
sections.content:
The Designated Expert reviews a request for required information. If any of it is missing, the expert shall not approve the registration to IANA.

For a Mandatory Extension Header (0-255), the request needs the value and name, the procedure for processing the header, a definition and intended use, and the size of the header (by default, the entire remaining payload).

For an Optional Extension Header (256-511), it needs the value and name, the processing procedure, a definition and intended use including any extension ordering requirements, and the range of allowable H-LEN values, which must be in the range 1-5.
sections.eli5: The referee has a checklist. If the form is missing any item, the new label is turned down.

sections.title: Private Use Range and Registry Note
sections.content:
RFC 7280 reserves the decimal range 144-159 (0x80-0x8F) for Private Use. IANA does not allocate these values. They suit experimental options, for example when no general-purpose solution was planned or there is too little operational experience to know whether a general one is needed.

This use is not coordinated between users, so the uniqueness of a value cannot be guaranteed. Authors of specifications MUST still contact IANA for a new value, because an IANA-allocated value uniquely identifies the method. Such an allocation is REQUIRED for any method that is to be standardised.

Section 4 records an additional explanatory note in the registry, placed before the existing note. It restates that 0-255 identifies Mandatory Extension Headers and 256-511 identifies Optional Extension Headers.
sections.eli5: A few labels are left open for anyone to scribble on while testing. They might clash with someone else's, so a real design must ask for its own official label.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it does not present new security considerations. It only changes how registry values are allocated and documented.
sections.eli5: Changing the rules for adding labels does not create any new danger.

viz.caption: THE TWO RANGES OF THE ULE NEXT-HEADER REGISTRY

Name, processing procedure, definition and use, size
